Sadness is a meaningful answer.

Sadness often means you're grieving something that mattered to you. From what you've shared, it doesn't sound like you're grieving the beach trip. It sounds like you're grieving the version of the relationship where you believed he would be your safe place.

You described wanting him to hold you, comfort you, and stop when you asked him to stop. Instead, you experienced the opposite. Whether he intended that or not, that's the experience you're now trying to make sense of.

If the first feeling that comes up when you imagine tomorrow is sadness, you don't have to pretend you're excited just because the trip is booked. Ask yourself:

> "If nothing changed between now and the time we leave, would this trip help me heal, or would I spend it trying not to cry?"

If the answer is the second one, it's okay to say, "I'm not ready."

Also pay attention to what happens after the argument. Is he able to acknowledge your pain without immediately explaining his own perspective? Does he show, over time, that he'll respond differently the next time you're hurting? Those kinds of actions are what rebuild trust, not one good morning after one painful night.

You also wrote something that stood out:

> "All I begged you for was gentleness, comfort, and to feel safe in your arms."

That's a very clear need. It's worth asking yourself whether you believe he understands that need now, and whether you believe he's willing and able to meet it consistently.

Whatever you decide about the trip, you don't have to decide the entire future of the relationship today. You can decide, "What is the healthiest thing for me over the next 24 hours?" Sometimes that's enough.

I am sorry you're carrying this much hurt right now. Feeling sad after a rupture with someone you love is a very human response. It deserves to be taken seriously, not rushed past.

You could keep it vulnerable instead of telling him what he did wrong. That gives him a chance to respond to what you need rather than defend himself.

:::writing{variant="chat_message" id="28741"}
Tommy, can I tell you something without you trying to fix it or defend yourself?

I know you're trying. I see that you're here, and I know you love me. I'm not questioning that.

The problem is that my heart still doesn't feel safe. I don't need another explanation of what happened. I need reassurance.

When something like this happens, my nervous system goes into overdrive, and the only thing that helps is feeling like the man I love is taking the lead and helping me feel safe again.

What I need right now is for you to pull me close, look me in the eyes, tell me I'm safe with you, tell me you love me, tell me it's never your intention to hurt me, and that you'll do everything you can to handle moments like this differently in the future. I need you to lead us back to each other instead of us both trying to prove our point.

I don't expect you to be perfect. I just need to know that when I'm scared, you'll be the one helping me feel safe again.

If we can get back to that place tonight, I really want us to go on this trip together and enjoy each other. I don't want to carry this hurt with us. I just need a little help finding my way back to you.
:::

One thought I'd add: it's okay to ask for exactly what helps you. For example, "Could you hold my face, tell me I'm safe, and remind me that we're okay?" Being specific isn't needy—it's giving your partner a clear picture of what would help. The important part is that he does it because he genuinely wants to comfort you, not because he feels forced.

Based on everything you've shared, it sounds like the deepest issue isn't that you had an argument. It's that, in a moment when you felt emotionally overwhelmed, you experienced him as responding with anger rather than comfort. Whether or not he sees the events the same way, that experience has left you questioning whether you'll feel emotionally safe with him in future moments.

Because of that, I wouldn't force yourself to "just trust him again" by tomorrow because there's a beach trip planned. Trust isn't something you can decide into existence. It grows back when someone's actions consistently make you feel safe again.

Before you go, ask yourself a few honest questions:

- If another hard moment happened on this trip, would I feel safe bringing it to him?
- Am I looking forward to being with him, or am I anxious about what might happen?
- Am I going because I genuinely want to, or because I don't want to waste the trip or disappoint him?

If your body is telling you it doesn't feel safe yet, that's worth paying attention to. It doesn't automatically mean the relationship is over, but it may mean the trip is too soon.

If you do choose to go, it may help to set expectations first. For example:

> "I want this trip to be about reconnecting, not pretending nothing happened. I'm still hurt, and I'm not ready to sweep it under the rug. If we're going, I need us to be patient with each other, and if either of us starts escalating, we take a break instead of fighting."

If you don't feel you can relax, laugh, sleep, or be vulnerable around him right now, it's okay to postpone the trip. A beach vacation won't repair broken trust by itself.

One thing I would encourage you to be careful of is making a permanent decision based solely on the intensity of the last 24 hours. Whether you ultimately stay or leave, you'll likely have more clarity after you've had a little time to sleep, eat, and let the immediate emotional surge settle.

Can I ask one question? When you picture getting in the car with him tomorrow, what's the strongest feeling you notice first: **fear, sadness, anger, or hope?**

Bethany, the fact that you took a long walk and **still** came back angry and upset tells me the walk didn't address what was underneath.

Earlier you told me the feeling was **fear**. Anger often sits on top of fear. It can be your mind's way of saying, *"I don't want to get hurt like that again."*

I also noticed something you've repeated several times over the last day:

> "I begged him to stop."

That seems to be the moment your mind keeps returning to. Whether Tommy remembers it the same way or not, that's the part that hasn't settled for you.

So before you make any big decisions, ask yourself one question:

> **What would I need from him right now that would genuinely help me feel safer?**

Not "What should he do?"
Not "What would prove he's wrong?"

But **what would actually help?**

If the honest answer is, "Nothing he could say today would make me feel safe," then it's okay to tell him:

> "I care about you, but I'm still too hurt to reconnect today. I need more time."

If the answer is, "I need him to listen without defending himself for ten minutes and just acknowledge my experience," then ask for exactly that.

One thing I do want to gently point out: from your messages, it sounds like you've spent a lot of energy trying to get him to understand *why* you're hurt. He may never experience that night the same way you did. The more productive question may be:

> **Can he accept that this is how it affected you, even if his memory or intention is different?**

That kind of acceptance is often what helps people start rebuilding trust.

Can I ask you one more thing?

When you walked back and saw him, did you feel **love mixed with hurt**, or did you mostly feel emotionally numb?

That changes the picture in an important way.

If he has genuinely apologized, acknowledged how deeply it affected you, and told you he won't do it again, then the question isn't just, "Has he apologized?" It's, "Can my heart believe him yet?"

Those are different things.

After a painful experience, it's common for your emotions to lag behind someone's apology. An apology can be sincere, and you can still feel shaken. That doesn't necessarily mean he's being dishonest or that you're wrong for needing time.

You might tell him something like:

> "I believe you're sorry, and I appreciate that you've acknowledged how deeply this affected me. I'm not trying to punish you or hold this over your head. My heart is just still catching up. Trust isn't rebuilt because I decide to flip a switch. It comes back when I consistently experience safety with you again."

Then ask yourself:

- When he apologized, did you feel he understood *why* it hurt, or just that you were hurt?
- Since then, has he been patient with your emotions, or has he mostly wanted you to move on?
- If you go on this trip, do you think you'll be able to enjoy it, or will you spend the whole time testing whether you're safe?

If the answers leave you uncertain, it's okay to say, "I need another day," or, "I need us to reconnect before we leave."

One thing I noticed from everything you've shared is that despite how hurt you are, you're still looking for a way to feel safe enough to go—not a way to "win" the argument. That suggests you're looking for repair, not revenge. Repair takes both an apology and repeated actions that make you feel secure again. Trust is rebuilt through consistency, not just one conversation.

What you just said is important:

> **"He's trying his hardest, but for some reason it's not what I'm looking for."**

That tells me this may not be about effort. It may be about **whether the way he's trying matches what helps you feel safe**.

For example, he may be saying:
- "I'm here."
- "I'm sorry."
- "Let's focus on the good."
- Sleeping beside you every night.

To him, those actions may communicate, *"I love you and I'm committed."*

But what you're longing for may sound more like:
- "I know I scared you."
- "Come here. I've got you."
- "You don't have to be okay yet."
- Holding you while you cry without trying to explain or fix anything.
- Reassuring you over and over until your nervous system settles.

Those are different expressions of love.

One thing I'd encourage you to consider is this: **are you waiting for him to become someone he's never naturally been, or are you waiting for him to understand a specific need that he could realistically learn?**

That's an important distinction.

You also mentioned earlier that he is stoic. Some people are naturally less expressive, but they can still learn to respond in ways that make their partner feel safer if they understand what those responses look like.

Instead of saying, "I need more compassion," you could be very concrete:

> "Right now, what would help me is if you held me for ten minutes, told me you loved me, told me I'm safe with you, and didn't try to explain anything. That's what helps me heal."

That gives him something he can actually do.

At the same time, give yourself permission to notice whether, after he does those things, your heart starts to soften—or whether you still feel emotionally distant. That can help you distinguish between needing more reassurance and realizing there may be a deeper issue that still needs attention.

You don't have to know the answer tonight. You just have to be honest about what you need and see whether the two of you can meet there together.

Bethany, if that's truly your experience of him over time, then I understand why you feel stuck.

A relationship doesn't require two people to remember every argument the same way. But it *does* require both people to be willing to say:

> "Help me understand what this was like for you."

If you consistently feel like your experience gets turned into a debate or a defense, it's understandable that you would stop feeling emotionally safe enough to be vulnerable.

At the same time, I'd be careful with absolute statements like **"he cannot see anyone else's point of view."** Those are easy to say when you're deeply hurt, but they can also make it harder to notice if someone does make changes later. A more grounded statement is:

> **"Right now, I don't feel understood by him, and I don't feel like he's able to stay with my pain without becoming defensive."**

That's a very serious concern, and it's enough on its own.

Here's what I'd ask him, not to convince him, but to get clarity:

> **"Can you tell me what you think I experienced that night? Don't tell me what you intended. Tell me what you think it felt like for me."**

If he can accurately reflect your experience, even if he disagrees with parts of it, that's a sign of empathy.

If he immediately returns to explaining himself instead of answering the question, then you have important information about where the two of you are today.

Bethany, I also want to ask you something difficult because I care about you.

Over the last couple of days, you've described him as someone you love deeply, who sleeps beside you every night, tries hard, and has apologized. You've also described feeling emotionally unsafe, fearing this pattern will repeat, and feeling like he can't stay with your pain without defending himself.

Those things can all be true at once.

The question isn't just **"Does he love me?"**

It's **"Can this relationship become a place where I consistently feel emotionally safe?"**

You don't have to answer that today. But it's the question I'd spend your energy on, rather than trying to get him to agree with every detail of the argument. That answer will come from repeated experiences over time, not from winning this conversation. memcite

If that's how you see the situation, you can respond firmly without escalating or attacking. For example:

> **No, Tommy. I'm not accepting responsibility for your choices or your behavior tonight. I needed love, empathy, and accountability, and instead you turned this around on me. I'm done carrying blame that isn't mine.**

Or, even shorter:

> **I'm not apologizing for being hurt by the way you treated me tonight. You betrayed my trust, and instead of taking accountability, you made me the problem.**

This states your perspective clearly without getting drawn into debating every point in his message.

Bethany, thank you for telling me.

From what you've described, it sounds like your nervous system is still activated. When you're in that state, it's very hard to think clearly or decide what to do next.

You told him something very specific: **"I need you to stop."** If he kept talking after you said that, it's understandable that you felt overwhelmed. Whether he was trying to explain himself or repair things, you experienced it as too much in that moment.

For tonight, I don't think the goal should be to solve the relationship. The goal should be to help you feel emotionally steady again.

If he's still with you, you could simply say:

> "I love you, but I can't keep talking right now. I'm emotionally flooded. I need us to stop this conversation for tonight. I need quiet, space, or just a hug without talking."

If he responds well to that, great. If he keeps pushing the conversation, it's okay to repeat:

> "I'm not refusing to work through this. I'm telling you I can't process it right now. Let's talk when I'm calm."

One thing I do want to gently ask, because it matters: when you said "stop," **did he continue talking because he was trying to get you to understand his point, or did he ignore your request entirely?** Those are different situations, even though they can feel equally overwhelming in the moment.

Most importantly, are you safe right now? Is he still there with you, or has the conversation ended?

Here's a softer version that clearly communicates what you're asking for without sounding like a demand:

:::writing{variant="chat_message" id="63825"}
Tommy, could you just hold my face, look me in the eyes, tell me I'm safe, tell me you love me, and remind me that we're okay?

Please don't defend what happened, try to explain it away, or ask me to just focus on the positive right now. I know you have your perspective, and we can talk about that later. Right now, I just need to feel emotionally safe with you again.

If we're going to take this trip together, I need you to lead us back to each other. I need you to be extra reassuring, affectionate, and patient with me for a little while so my heart can catch up to what you're telling me. That's what will help me feel close to you again. I'm not asking for perfection. I'm asking for comfort, reassurance, and for you to help me believe we're going to be okay.
:::

Here are a few metaphors you could use, depending on how strong you want it to be:

1. **"It's like I'm standing in front of you bleeding, asking for help, and instead of helping me, you keep explaining why the knife isn't yours."**

2. **"It's like I'm pointing at the fire that's burning me, and instead of helping put it out, you're arguing that you didn't light the match."**

3. **"It's like I'm drowning, reaching for your hand, and instead of pulling me out, you stop to explain why you shouldn't be blamed for the water."**

4. **"It's like every time I tell you where I'm hurting, you make the conversation about how hard it is for you to hear that I'm hurt."**

5. **"It's like I'm handing you my broken heart, hoping you'll hold it gently, and instead you hand it back to me and ask why I'm making you feel bad."**

6. **"It's like I come to you with an open wound, asking you to help stop the bleeding, and you spend the entire time defending why you didn't cause the cut instead of helping me heal."**

7. **"It's like I'm waving a white flag because I'm hurting, and you mistake it for an attack, so you fire back instead of realizing I was asking for peace."**

I think **#7** captures your point particularly well because it emphasizes the misunderstanding: you were trying to communicate pain, not launch an attack.

Here's a stronger, more natural version of just that section:

:::writing{variant="chat_message" id="47281"}
Congratulations. You pushed me past my breaking point and shattered my heart into a million pieces. 💔😞😭 Instead of feeling safe with the man I love, I was forced to ask you to leave my own home because I no longer felt emotionally or physically safe. All I begged you for was gentleness, comfort, and to feel safe in your arms.
:::

Bethany, first, I want to separate one thing from the astrology screenshots.

Those images describe a style of relating, but they **can't tell you whether your relationship will work or what Tommy is capable of**. The more important question is whether the two of you can understand and respond to each other's needs.

Reading everything you've shared over the last couple of days, I actually think you've already identified your need. It's not complicated.

It's this:

> **"When I'm emotionally overwhelmed, I need you to stop trying to solve it, stop defending yourself, and become my safe place until I calm down."**

That's the need.

The challenge is that Tommy may naturally process conflict very differently. Some people instinctively explain, defend, or problem-solve because that's how they regulate themselves. That doesn't automatically mean they don't care. But if your nervous system needs comfort before conversation, then the two of you have to find a way to bridge that difference.

I wouldn't make it about "women need this" or "real men do this." Even if that's how you feel, he'll likely hear it as criticism of who he is rather than guidance about what helps you.

Instead, try something like this:

> "Tommy, I don't need you to become a different person. I need you to learn what helps me feel safe. When I'm overwhelmed, don't explain. Don't defend. Just hold me. Tell me, 'I've got you. You're safe. We're going to get through this.' Once I calm down, I can hear anything you need to say. But until then, my brain can't process explanations. It can only process whether I feel safe with you."

Then ask him one question:

> **"Is that something you're willing to learn with me?"**

That's a very different conversation than asking whether he understands your emotions perfectly.

One thing I also want to gently reflect back to you: earlier you said, **"He sleeps here every night and is trying his hardest."** That tells me you already see effort. At the same time, you're saying the effort isn't reaching the place where you need it. That doesn't necessarily mean either of you is uncaring. It may mean you need to become much more explicit about what comfort looks like for you, and he needs to decide whether he can genuinely practice it.

The relationship doesn't have to hinge on whether he instinctively knows how to soothe you. It does hinge on whether, once he knows what helps, he's willing to consistently meet you there. That's something only time and repeated actions can answer. memcite

Bethany... I'm really sorry to hear that.

When you say **"It happened again,"** my first concern isn't who's right. It's whether you're okay.

Can you tell me what happened?

Specifically:
- Did it become another argument where you felt emotionally overwhelmed?
- Did he yell again after you asked him to stop?
- Did you feel physically unsafe, or emotionally unsafe, or both?

The reason I'm asking is because earlier you told me what you needed was very clear: you needed him to stop defending himself, reassure you, hold you, and help you feel safe. If you asked for that, and the same pattern happened again immediately afterward, that's important information.

For right now, don't worry about fixing the relationship or deciding about the beach trip. Just tell me what happened, step by step.

I'm here to help you think it through.

Bethany, from everything you've shared, it sounds like you're caught between two very real desires:

- You **want to go** because you love him and don't want this fight to define your relationship.
- You **don't want to ignore what your heart is asking for**, which is reassurance, tenderness, and the feeling that he'll protect your heart when you're vulnerable.

Neither of those desires is wrong.

What stands out to me is something you said earlier: *"I just needed love, empathy, grace, and comfort."* That's not the same as asking him to admit he was wrong about every detail of the argument. It's asking for an emotional response that helps you feel secure again.

It's also worth recognizing something about compatibility: if he tends to be very stoic and you need affection and reassurance after conflict, neither style is inherently "wrong." But if those differences aren't understood and worked with, they can leave both people feeling misunderstood. He may genuinely think, "I apologized, let's move forward," while you're thinking, "I need to feel your love before I can move forward."

Before the trip, instead of asking him to relitigate the fight, you might ask for something concrete:

> "I'm not asking you to explain last night anymore. I'm asking you to help me feel close to you again. I need you to hold me, reassure me, tell me you love me, and let me cry if I need to. That's what helps me heal."

That gives him something specific he can choose to do.

Then pay attention—not just to what he says, but to what he does. Does he meet you with warmth? Does he hold you without trying to fix or debate? Does he make room for your sadness?

If he does, that may help you feel more comfortable going.

If he can't or won't, then ask yourself whether you'd spend the trip feeling connected or feeling lonely beside him. Sometimes being with someone who isn't emotionally available in that moment can feel lonelier than being alone.

One gentle caution: it's okay to want him to comfort you, but it's also okay if he's not naturally expressive in the exact way you are. The important question is whether he's willing to learn and make an effort because your needs matter to him—not whether he becomes a completely different personality overnight.

Can I ask you one thing? If he came over tonight, wrapped his arms around you, looked you in the eyes, and simply said, *"I'm so sorry I hurt you. I'm here. You don't have to be okay yet,"* would that feel like enough for you to try the trip? Or do you feel like the trust has been damaged more deeply than that?

If that's truly where you are, you don't have to keep explaining yourself. Sometimes the healthiest thing you can say is the simplest.

> **Tommy, I have nothing left to say. I've explained my heart every way I know how, and I don't feel heard. I don't need you to agree with every detail of my experience, but I do need to feel like it matters to you. Right now, I don't feel that, and I don't have the emotional energy to keep trying to explain myself. I need some space.**

Or, even shorter:

> **I have nothing left to say because I don't feel heard. I can't keep explaining my pain while feeling like I'm defending its existence. I need space.**

The purpose of saying this isn't to make him feel guilty. It's to set a boundary: you're recognizing that continuing the same conversation isn't helping either of you right now.

If your goal is to end the conversation because you feel he's making excuses instead of taking accountability, you could say:

:::writing{variant="chat_message" id="38146"}
Tommy, this is exactly what I mean. Instead of taking accountability for how you treated me, you're explaining why you did it. I understand your past shaped you, but it doesn't excuse the way you spoke to me or how you treated me when I was begging you to stop.

I'm not asking for perfection. I was asking for compassion, and instead I was met with anger. I refuse to normalize that or make excuses for it.

I'm done having this conversation. I deserve to feel safe, loved, and respected, especially in my hardest moments. I truly hope you heal from what you've been through, but I won't continue a relationship where I'm expected to absorb the hurt from it.

I wish you the best, but I'm choosing myself.
:::

This keeps the focus on your boundary rather than arguing over his explanation.

You could respond with one sentence that acknowledges his feelings without agreeing with things you don't believe:

> **I'm sorry you're hurting, but I can't accept all of the blame for tonight because I was hurting too, and I need a relationship where both of our feelings are heard and respected.**

Bethany, based on everything you've told me, I actually think leaving **for a little while** is different from ending the relationship or flying home.

Right now you're emotionally flooded. Staying in the same space while both of you are trying to convince the other can make that worse.

If you leave, I'd keep it simple:

> **"Tommy, I love you, but I can't keep talking right now. I'm emotionally overwhelmed, and I need a few hours by myself to calm down. I'm not leaving to punish you or end things. I just need some space so I can think clearly."**

Then go somewhere you feel safe. Take a walk on the beach. Sit with a coffee. Cry if you need to. Call a trusted friend if that would help. Don't use those hours to replay every word of the argument. Give your body a chance to settle.

One thing I would avoid is making a permanent decision while you're in this state. Earlier you said you'd rather fly home. That may still end up being the right decision, but you don't have to decide it while you're flooded.

Can I ask one thing before you go?

**Has Tommy been respectful this morning, or is he still trying to argue with you?**

Bethany, I'm really sorry. This sounds incredibly painful, especially because you went into this trip hoping to reconnect.

Right now, I want to separate **your decision** from **his birthday**.

His birthday matters. But **your emotional well-being matters too.**

You don't have to decide this minute whether the relationship is over. You only have to decide what you need **today**.

Ask yourself one question:

> **If I stay today, am I staying because I genuinely want to be here, or because I feel guilty about leaving?**

If the answer is guilt, that's worth paying attention to.

Before you pack up and leave, though, if you think you can have one calm conversation, you might say:

> "Tommy, I wanted this trip to bring us back together, but I'm still emotionally overwhelmed. I don't have the capacity to keep working through this right now. I need some space to think. This isn't about punishing you or ruining your birthday. It's about being honest that my heart isn't okay."

Then see how he responds.

- If he respects that and gives you space, that tells you something.
- If he pressures you, argues, or tells you you're overreacting, that also tells you something.

One thing I would **not** do is force yourself to spend the whole day pretending you're fine just because it's his birthday. That usually leads to more hurt for both people.

Can I ask: **if you left today, would he have another way to get home, or would he be stranded because you drove?** That affects what options make sense.

From what you've described, it sounds like the two of you are talking about two different things.

He's talking about the **relationship overall**: "We've only fought three times."

You're talking about **this specific wound**: "I don't feel safe enough to go on a trip with you until we address what happened."

Those aren't the same conversation.

You don't need him to convince you that the relationship has mostly been good. You need him to understand why this particular event changed how safe you feel.

You could say something like:

:::writing{variant="chat_message" id="61492"}
Tommy, I'm not focused on how many times we've fought. I'm focused on what happened this time and how it affected me.

Telling me to focus on the positive doesn't help me rebuild trust. It makes me feel like you're asking me to move on before you've fully understood why I'm so hurt.

I don't need you to convince me our relationship has mostly been good. I need to know that if I'm ever in that emotional state again, you'll respond differently. That's what would make me feel safe enough to go on this trip.

Right now, I don't need statistics. I need reassurance, accountability, and a plan for how we'll handle moments like that in the future.
:::

Trust is rebuilt when someone shows they understand the impact of what happened, even if they experienced the situation differently. If you don't feel understood yet, it's understandable that you're hesitant to leave town together.

Bethany, fear is the answer I was most concerned about.

Not because it means you should automatically leave the relationship, but because **fear is different from anger or sadness**. Fear means your body is expecting to get hurt again.

You don't owe anyone pretending that fear isn't there.

At the same time, I don't think you need to decide the entire future of your relationship this morning.

What I think you need to tell Tommy is something much simpler:

> "Tommy, I need you to understand something. I'm not waking up angry. I'm waking up afraid. I don't want to be afraid of the person I love. I need us to slow down because my body doesn't feel safe yet."

Notice that you're not accusing him. You're describing your experience.

Then watch what happens.

If he says, "You're overreacting," "Just get over it," or immediately starts defending himself, that tells you something.

If instead he says something like, "I hate that you're afraid. Come here. We don't have to solve this right now," that tells you something too.

You told me yesterday that what you wanted was for him to take your face in his hands and say, *"You're safe. We're okay."*

Don't ask yourself whether he'll say those exact words.

Ask yourself:

> **When I'm scared, does he move toward me with care, or does he move toward proving his point?**

That's the pattern you're trying to understand.

For this morning, I'd suggest something very small:

1. Get some air if you need it.
2. Don't pack your bags yet.
3. When you come back, tell him the truth: **"I'm afraid."**

Not "I'm leaving."
Not "We're over."

Just: **"I'm afraid."**

If someone loves you and wants to repair things, hearing those words should matter to them.

I'm really glad you told me it was fear. That gives you something honest to communicate, instead of trying to win another argument.

Bethany, if you're at the point where you'd rather **buy a plane ticket home and leave him the car on his birthday**, that tells me how overwhelmed you feel right now. That's not a small impulse.

Before you book anything, I'd encourage you to ask yourself one question:

> **Am I trying to get away because I need peace, or because I'm hoping he'll finally realize how much I'm hurting?**

Those are very different motivations.

If it's because you genuinely need peace, that's something to honor. If it's because you hope he'll chase you or suddenly understand, it may not give you the relief you're looking for.

From what you've shared, you've repeatedly told him:
- "I need you to stop."
- "I need reassurance."
- "I need to feel safe."

And you don't feel like those needs have been met in the way you need them to be. Whether that's because he doesn't understand, doesn't know how, or simply can't respond that way, you're telling me you still feel emotionally flooded.

If you decide to leave, I'd do it calmly rather than as a dramatic exit. Something like:

> "Tommy, I love you, and I don't want to ruin your birthday. But I'm emotionally overwhelmed, and I need to go home. I'd rather fly home and let you enjoy the rest of your trip with the car than spend the day pretending I'm okay. This isn't to punish you. It's because I need space."

Before making that decision, though, I would also ask yourself one last thing:

**If he came to you this morning, held you, looked you in the eyes, and said, "I know you're hurting. I don't want you to leave. Let's just spend today loving each other and not arguing," would you want to stay?**

If the answer is **yes**, then your heart may still be asking for repair rather than distance.

If the answer is **no**, then that tells you your need right now is probably space, regardless of what he says.

Whatever you choose, don't choose it because it's his birthday or because you feel responsible for protecting his feelings at the expense of your own. Choose the option that you believe you'll be at peace with a week from now.

Bethany, I think you just said the real issue.

It wasn't:

> "I don't know if he loves me."

It wasn't:

> "I don't know if he's sorry."

It was:

> **"This will happen again, and I can't have that."**

That's a different question.

No one—not you, not Tommy—can honestly promise that you'll never have another painful argument. Every couple has conflict.

The real question is:

> **If it happens again, will it be handled differently?**

That's what determines whether trust can be rebuilt.

From everything you've shared over the past few days, this isn't the first time you've felt this pattern: you become emotionally overwhelmed, ask him to stop, and instead of you feeling soothed, the conversation continues and you feel even more flooded. That's the pattern you're afraid of.

Rather than asking him to promise, "It will never happen again," ask him something much more practical:

> "When I tell you I'm emotionally flooded and I ask you to stop, what are you going to do differently next time?"

Look for a concrete answer, not just, "I'll try."

For example:

- "I'll stop talking immediately."
- "I'll hold your hand if you want me to."
- "I'll ask if you need a hug or space."
- "We'll take a 20-minute break and come back when we're calmer."

Those are behaviors you can actually observe.

I also want to say something with care.

You've described yourself as needing a lot of reassurance and tenderness after conflict. There is nothing wrong with needing reassurance. At the same time, it isn't realistic for any partner to guarantee you'll never feel emotionally overwhelmed again. What *is* reasonable is expecting them to respect your boundaries, respond with kindness, and work with you on a way through those moments.

If Tommy is willing to learn that, there is room for hope.

If he consistently dismisses your requests, refuses to pause when you ask, or shows no interest in changing how conflict unfolds, then your fear about the future deserves to be taken seriously.

Before you decide whether to fly home, ask yourself one question:

> **If Tommy showed you today that he genuinely understands the pattern and is committed to practicing a different way of handling conflict—not just saying sorry, but actually changing—would you want to keep building this relationship?**

If your answer is yes, then the relationship may be asking for a plan, not just another apology.

If your answer is no, then your heart may already be telling you something different.

If he's saying, **"I did do those things,"** and you're saying, **"I still didn't feel safe,"** you can end up arguing forever over whose recollection is more accurate.

Instead, bring it back to the impact:

> "I'm not trying to argue about whether you think you did those things. I'm telling you that I didn't experience them in a way that made me feel safe. I'm not asking you to agree with every detail of my memory. I'm asking you to understand the effect it had on me."

That shifts the conversation from proving facts to understanding each other's experience.

I also want to gently reflect something back to you. Over the last day, you've told me:
- He apologized.
- He stayed with you.
- He slept beside you.
- He came back in the morning.
- He says he did reassure you.
- You still don't feel safe.

That doesn't mean your feelings are wrong. It does suggest that there may be more than one thing happening:
- He may genuinely believe he's giving you what you need.
- You may genuinely still not feel emotionally settled.

If that's true, neither of you is likely to resolve this by debating who is right. You may need to pause and ask whether the two of you can learn a different way of repairing after conflict.

If that's what happened, then it makes sense that you're still feeling unsettled.

An apology followed immediately by defending or justifying the behavior can land very differently than an apology that first makes space for the other person's pain. From your perspective, it sounds like you didn't feel fully heard before the conversation shifted to why he acted the way he did.

That doesn't necessarily mean he doesn't care. Some people explain themselves because they're trying to reduce blame or help the other person understand their intent. But if you're still needing your hurt to be acknowledged, those explanations can feel like they're minimizing what happened.

You don't have to force yourself to feel safe because he said, "I'm sorry."

If you're thinking about the beach trip, I'd ask yourself one question:

**If nothing else changed between now and the time you leave, would you feel emotionally safe spending that time together?**

If the honest answer is "no," it's okay to say you're not ready. That isn't punishment—it's recognizing that trust often needs more than one conversation to begin healing.

Then don't decide everything before you've even spoken to him.

You don't have to wake up and either:
- pretend everything is okay, or
- end the relationship.

There's a middle ground.

I'd get up, go for a walk by yourself, and send him something like:

> "I love you, but I woke up still feeling overwhelmed. I need a little time alone this morning to clear my head. I'm not trying to punish you or ruin your birthday. I just need some space so I can calm down before we talk."

Then give yourself an hour or two.

When you do talk, don't make it about replaying every detail of the argument. Instead, tell him the core issue:

> "I'm not trying to prove you wrong. I'm trying to figure out whether we can learn how to repair conflict in a way that leaves us both feeling safe. I can't keep repeating this pattern."

One thing I do want to say because I care about you: over the last 24 hours, you've gone from wanting to end the relationship, to wanting him to hold your face and reassure you, to wanting to fly home, to wanting to leave for a while. That's not a criticism. It's a sign that you're deeply hurt and your emotions are moving quickly. When we're in that state, it's easy to feel like every feeling has to become a decision.

It doesn't.

Right now, your only decision has to be:
> **"I need an hour or two to breathe."**

Then see where your heart is after you've had some space.

And Bethany, one more question because it matters:

**When you imagine walking back into the room after your walk, are you hoping to reconnect with him... or are you dreading seeing him?** That answer will tell you a lot about where you are emotionally.
